t: A1. Animals aren't rational.
s: Rationality isn't what makes suffering matter, and the criterion would exclude humans who lack it
k: They don't think Animals act on instinct Only humans are self-aware Sentience and moral status

t: A2. Humans are superior, so we can use the inferior.
s: Superior abilities give no right to dominate
k: We're the dominant species Man is the king of creation If they were superior, they'd eat us Sentience and moral status

t: A3. Animals don't have language.
s: An irrelevant criterion for pain; it excludes babies and non-verbal people
k: They can't talk If they suffered, they'd complain They can't say what they feel Sentience and moral status

t: A4. Animals don't have souls.
s: An unfalsifiable premise used as a public criterion
k: Animals have no spirit Only man was made in the image of God When they die, that's it Sentience and moral status

t: A5. Animals aren't conscious and don't feel pain like we do.
s: Contradicts the neuroscientific evidence (Cambridge Declaration, 2012; New York Declaration, 2024)
k: It's just a reflex Animal pain is different They're biological machines Sentience and moral status

t: A6. Fish and invertebrates don't feel pain.
s: Growing evidence of sentience in fish, cephalopods and decapods
k: Fish don't feel anything Fish have a three-second memory Shrimp don't even have a brain Sentience and moral status

t: A7. No duties, no rights.
s: Confuses moral agents with moral patients; it would exclude children
k: Animals don't pay taxes Would a lion respect your rights? Rights are for those in the social contract Sentience and moral status

t: A8. Animals aren't persons.
s: A persuasive definition: pick the concept that excludes them, then conclude they are excluded
k: Animals are things, not people They're objects, not subjects A person is someone who is self-aware Sentience and moral status

t: A9. Rights are a human invention, only for humans.
s: Genetic fallacy: where a norm came from doesn't set how far it reaches
k: Human rights are for humans Animals don't have a social security number Nature doesn't know about rights Sentience and moral status

t: A10. They're just animals.
s: Explicit speciesism: species membership as a moral criterion, like race in racism
k: It's just a chicken Come on, it's an animal Humans are humans, animals are animals Sentience and moral status

t: A11. It's normal for humans to be rational.
s: Treats individuals by what others have, not by what they have
k: People with disabilities are still human What counts is human nature, not the individual case Sentience and moral status

t: A12. Human babies have the potential to be rational.
s: Potential doesn't confer the rights of the actual, and it doesn't cover humans without potential
k: The baby will grow up and reason A cow will never be more than a cow Sentience and moral status

t: A13. It's natural to put our own first.
s: Partiality lets us prefer our own; it does not let us exploit others
k: My family first, then everyone else Would you save your child or a pig? Species is family Sentience and moral status

t: A14. Plants feel too.
s: No nervous system and no evidence of experience; and if they did feel, animal farming kills more plants
k: Doesn't lettuce suffer? I read that plants communicate Carrot murderer Sentience and moral status

t: A15. Where do you draw the line? Insects? Bacteria?
s: Continuum fallacy: a fuzzy boundary doesn't erase clear cases
k: What about the bacteria you kill washing your hands? Do ants count too? If everything matters, nothing matters Sentience and moral status

t: A16. Killing without pain isn't harm.
s: Death takes away good future experiences; the same holds for humans with no sense of time
k: If it didn't suffer, what's the problem? They don't know they're going to die They have no sense of the future Sentience and moral status

t: A17. Animals are property.
s: Describes a legal status; doesn't justify it (as with slavery)
k: The cow is mine, I'll do what I want I bought it, it's mine It's a product like any other Sentience and moral status

t: A18. What matters is the species, not the individual.
s: Species don't feel; individuals do
k: Chickens aren't endangered As long as the species exists, it's fine We protect ecosystems, not every animal Sentience and moral status

t: A19. Vegans anthropomorphize animals.
s: Denying similar mental states is also an error (anthropodenial), and the evidence contradicts it
k: You've watched too much Disney You're projecting feelings That's sentimentality Sentience and moral status

t: A20. Humans have intrinsic value; animals have instrumental value.
s: Circular: it assumes the conclusion
k: Only humans have dignity Animals are means, not ends An animal is worth what it gives us Sentience and moral status

t: A21. I respect animals, but humans come first
s: A special status no one explains and that wouldn't pass the veil of ignorance: the weight should depend on the size of the harm, not on species
k: Humans have dignity, animals don't Human life is worth more Animals matter, but less Sentience and moral status

t: A22. Humans suffer more than animals
s: Suffering more in some cases doesn't license ignoring those who suffer less; and less cognition often means more suffering and more vulnerability
k: Humans suffer more because they understand what is happening Human suffering is deeper Sentience and moral status

t: A23. Morality exists to protect us from each other
s: It would also exclude babies and vulnerable people; and explaining where a practice came from does not justify it
k: Ethics was invented for self-protection Animals can't threaten us, so they're not part of the deal Sentience and moral status

t: A24. Species is biology, race is a social construct
s: A biological criterion can be as unjust as a social one: what makes discrimination unjust is giving someone's interests biased weight
k: Speciesism isn't like racism Race doesn't exist, species does Sentience and moral status

t: B1. There is humane slaughter.
s: A contradiction in terms: there is no compassionate way to kill someone who does not want to die
k: Slaughter is painless nowadays They are stunned first There is ethical meat Harm, death and welfare

t: B2. Free-range animals are happy.
s: They're still killed young; labels have little to do with practice, and changing the scale doesn't change the act
k: Free-range hens live happy lives Grass-fed cattle have a good life I only buy free-range eggs I buy from small farmers I buy from the local butcher My uncle raises them on his farm Family-farm meat is different Harm, death and welfare

t: B4. The problem is the industry, not consumers.
s: The industry exists to meet demand: system and consumer sustain each other
k: I'm against factory farming, not meat Change the system, not my plate It's the companies' and the system's fault Change the big corporations, not my dinner Consumers have no power Harm, death and welfare

t: B5. They had a good life and a quick death.
s: A good life doesn't license taking it; the idea is absurd applied to dogs or humans
k: Better than dying in the wild They lived well and died without noticing Harm, death and welfare

t: B6. Without farming, these animals wouldn't even exist.
s: Bringing someone into existence gives no right to kill them
k: If no one ate them, there'd be no cows We're giving them life Vegans want chickens to go extinct Harm, death and welfare

t: B7. Milk and eggs don't kill anyone.
s: Male chicks and calves are discarded, and cows and hens are slaughtered when production drops
k: I'm vegetarian, that's enough The cow doesn't die to give milk An egg isn't a chicken Harm, death and welfare

t: B8. The law guarantees animal welfare.
s: Laws allow confinement, mutilations without anesthesia and the killing of newborns
k: There are inspections We have welfare standards If it were cruel, it'd be banned Harm, death and welfare

t: B9. Those videos are exceptions or staged.
s: Much of what they show is standard, legal industry practice
k: That's from another country They filmed the worst case It's activist propaganda Harm, death and welfare

t: B10. Stressed animals make bad meat, so farmers take good care of them.
s: The incentive is small and partial; it doesn't cover suffering that doesn't affect profit
k: No one would hurt their own profits Stressed meat is tough Harm, death and welfare

t: C1. It's natural to eat meat.
s: Appeal to nature: natural doesn't mean right
k: It's human nature We've always been hunters It's biological Nature, biology and evolution

t: C2. Lions eat other animals.
s: Lions aren't moral agents and have no alternative
k: That's how nature works Will you ask the lion to go vegan? Cats eat mice Nature, biology and evolution

t: C3. We have canine teeth; we are omnivores.
s: Being able to eat it isn't needing to; anatomy creates no duty
k: Look at my teeth Our gut is an omnivore gut If we were meant to be herbivores, we'd have four stomachs Nature, biology and evolution

t: C4. We're at the top of the food chain.
s: Ecologically false (the average human trophic level is about 2.2) and morally irrelevant
k: We're at the top for a reason We're predators It's the law of the food chain Nature, biology and evolution

t: C5. Eating meat made us evolve.
s: An adaptive past doesn't dictate present morality
k: Without meat we'd still be in the trees Our brains grew thanks to meat Nature, biology and evolution

t: C6. Might makes right.
s: Social Darwinism: it describes a process, not a norm
k: Survival of the fittest It's the law of the jungle The weak serve the strong Nature, biology and evolution

t: C7. It's the circle of life.
s: A euphemism: breeding, confining and slaughtering is an industry, not a natural cycle
k: It's the cycle of life Everything dies someday It's part of life Nature, biology and evolution

t: C8. If we don't eat them, animals will take over the planet.
s: Gets the cause backwards: there are so many because they're bred
k: Cows would take over There'd be chickens everywhere Nature, biology and evolution

t: C9. Farm animals exist for this.
s: An imposed purpose: the "function" is assigned by whoever profits
k: Cattle were born to become steak Broiler chickens were made for this It's their purpose Nature, biology and evolution

t: C10. Cows need to be milked.
s: Only because they were made pregnant and bred for overproduction
k: If you don't milk her, the cow suffers We're helping the cow Nature, biology and evolution

t: C11. We naturally crave meat.
s: A learned and reinforced preference; desire is no justification
k: It's the body asking for it The smell of a barbecue is irresistible for a reason Nature, biology and evolution

t: D1. We've always done it.
s: Appeal to tradition: the same phrase defended slavery and the subjugation of women
k: My ancestors ate meat It's been this way for thousands of years It's not going to change now Tradition, culture and religion

t: D2. It's cultural; criticizing it is ethnocentric.
s: Selective cultural relativism: not applied to practices the person condemns
k: You can't judge other cultures It's part of our regional identity That's cultural imperialism Tradition, culture and religion

t: D3. Indigenous and traditional peoples eat animals.
s: Uses those with no alternative to justify those who have one; veganism already says "as far as is possible and practicable"
k: What about Indigenous peoples? Will you tell Indigenous peoples they're wrong? Veganism is colonialist What about the Inuit, who have no alternative? What about people living in the Arctic? Not everywhere has a supermarket Tradition, culture and religion

t: D4. God gave us dominion over animals.
s: Many traditions read dominion as stewardship; and it is a theological premise, not a public one
k: It's in Genesis God made animals for man Who are you to contradict God? Tradition, culture and religion

t: D5. Jesus ate fish.
s: Appeal to authority; a historical context of necessity doesn't carry over
k: Jesus multiplied the fish In the Bible they sacrificed lambs Tradition, culture and religion

t: D6. Everybody eats meat.
s: Appeal to popularity: popular isn't right
k: You're a minority If it were wrong, nobody would do it Almost everyone eats meat Tradition, culture and religion

t: D7. It's legal; the law allows it.
s: Legalistic fallacy: the law follows morality, with a delay
k: If it's sold in the supermarket, it's allowed It's not a crime Tradition, culture and religion

t: D8. Barbecues bring the family together.
s: The bond is the gathering, not the animal
k: Sunday isn't Sunday without a barbecue It's a family tradition Christmas isn't Christmas without turkey Tradition, culture and religion

t: D9. My grandparents ate meat and lived to 90.
s: Anecdotal evidence and survivorship bias
k: My grandmother ate lard and lived to 100 Nobody had these diseases back then Tradition, culture and religion

t: D10. Great thinkers ate meat.
s: Appeal to authority; many also defended human hierarchies we now reject
k: Aristotle ate meat Einstein wasn't vegan Tradition, culture and religion

t: E1. It's my personal choice; don't impose your morals.
s: Personal choice ends where there is a victim; every rule against harm "imposes"
k: Everyone eats what they want Respect my plate I don't criticize your lettuce Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E2. Morality is relative.
s: Self-refuting and applied selectively; it confuses taste with a claim about harm to others
k: Morality is a social construct Right and wrong depend on who is looking Everyone has their own truth That's your opinion You think one thing, I think another Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E4. The state can't ban what I eat.
s: Switches from "is it wrong?" to "should it be banned?"
k: Vegans want to ban meat Vegan dictatorship Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E5. Everything in moderation.
s: False middle ground: moderation doesn't make an unjustifiable harm acceptable
k: Nothing to extremes Balance is the secret Extremes are bad Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E6. Nobody's perfect; I do what I can.
s: True in general, but used to avoid doing what is easy
k: I do my part Everyone at their own pace At least I recycle Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E7. I don't want to see those videos.
s: Willful ignorance: avoiding the information to avoid the obligation
k: Don't show me that at lunch I'd rather not know That's emotional terrorism Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E8. I love animals, but...
s: A contradiction between stated values and practice (the meat paradox)
k: I have three dogs I'm an animal lover, but I won't give up meat Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E9. Eating meat isn't an ideology; veganism is.
s: The dominant norm is invisible to those who follow it (carnism, Joy 2009)
k: Eating meat is normal, it's not a philosophy You're the ones politicizing food Carnism is a made-up word Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E10. Veganism is opinion, not science.
s: No moral position is "just science", including eating meat
k: That's ideology, not fact Science doesn't say eating meat is wrong Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E11. Even philosophers don't agree.
s: Disagreement isn't a tie; there is strong convergence against factory farming
k: It's an open debate Some philosophers defend eating meat Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E12. I know it's wrong, but I won't change.
s: Admitted weakness of will: concedes the moral point and refuses its consequence
k: You're right, but I like it too much Deep down I know I'll stop someday Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: E13. Defending animals is just utilitarianism
s: Equal consideration is a formal principle accepted by rival theories; knocking down utilitarianism doesn't rescue speciesism
k: That's Peter Singer, and utilitarianism is wrong It only makes sense in a utilitarian ethics Relativism, freedom and evasions

t: F1. On a desert island, would you eat an animal?
s: Extreme necessity doesn't justify the practice in normal conditions
k: What if you were starving? In an apocalypse you'd eat meat Edge cases and hypotheticals

t: F2. If a dog and a child were drowning, which would you save?
s: A preference in a tragic conflict doesn't license exploiting those who aren't in one
k: Your mother or a cow? Would you save your dog or a stranger? Edge cases and hypotheticals

t: F3. So should we stop lions from hunting?
s: Wild animal suffering is a serious question, and it does not favor eating animals
k: Will you lock up every predator? So nature is immoral? Edge cases and hypotheticals

t: F4. What about the insects you kill while driving?
s: Accidental, unavoidable harm differs from intentional, avoidable harm
k: You step on ants Your car kills mosquitoes Edge cases and hypotheticals

t: F6. What about the eggs from my rescued hen?
s: A rare, debatable case with no link to the industry; it doesn't legitimize buying
k: She lays them anyway What's wrong with that egg? Edge cases and hypotheticals

t: F7. Oysters and mussels don't feel.
s: Partly plausible; it confirms that sentience is the criterion
k: Oysters have no central nervous system Bivalves are almost plants Edge cases and hypotheticals

t: F8. What about meat that gets thrown away?
s: Eating without creating demand is a different case; it still reinforces seeing animals as food
k: If it'll be thrown out, better to eat it Party leftovers don't count Edge cases and hypotheticals

t: F9. You also kill mosquitoes and rats at home.
s: Self-defense and real conflict differ from breeding animals to eat
k: You use insect repellent If there's a cockroach, you kill it Edge cases and hypotheticals

t: G1. We need animal protein.
s: Protein needs are met by legumes, grains and soy
k: Where do you get your protein? Without meat you'll be weak You need quality protein Health and nutrition

t: G2. Plant protein is incomplete.
s: A 1970s myth; variety over the day provides all the essential amino acids
k: It lacks amino acids Plant protein has low biological value You have to combine everything in the same meal Health and nutrition

t: G3. If you need B12 supplements, it isn't natural.
s: Farm animals also get supplemented B12; and natural is not the criterion (C1)
k: A diet that needs pills is wrong No natural diet needs supplements Health and nutrition

t: G4. You'll lack iron, zinc and other micronutrients.
s: Plannable with a varied diet; iron deficiency is also common in meat eaters
k: Vegans are always anemic Iron from plants isn't absorbed Health and nutrition

t: G5. Milk is necessary for your bones.
s: Calcium is found in plants and fortified foods
k: Milk makes bones strong You'll get osteoporosis Children need milk Health and nutrition

t: G6. Only fish provides omega-3.
s: Fish get their DHA from algae, a direct source available to us
k: You have to eat fish twice a week Flaxseed doesn't give you DHA Health and nutrition

t: G7. Soy causes female hormones and cancer.
s: Phytoestrogens aren't estrogen; meta-analyses don't support the myth
k: Soy feminizes men Soy causes breast cancer Soy is GMO poison Health and nutrition

t: G8. Children and pregnant women can't be vegan.
s: Major nutrition bodies consider it appropriate at every life stage, with planning
k: That's child abuse The baby won't develop Pregnant women need meat Health and nutrition

t: G9. Athletes need meat.
s: There are elite vegan athletes; adequate protein intake is what matters
k: Nobody builds muscle without meat There's no such thing as a vegan bodybuilder Health and nutrition

t: G10. I know someone who got sick being vegan.
s: Anecdotal evidence; it confuses a badly planned diet with a vegan diet
k: My cousin got sick An influencer quit veganism for health reasons I saw an ex-vegan's story Health and nutrition

t: G11. My body can't adapt.
s: The blood type diet has been refuted; individual complaints are rarely investigated
k: I tried and felt sick My blood type needs meat Everybody is different Health and nutrition

t: G12. A carnivore, paleo or keto diet is healthiest.
s: Weak, short-term evidence that contradicts the large cohort studies
k: The carnivore diet cured my illness Our ancestors ate only meat Carbs are the villain Health and nutrition

t: G13. The WHO exaggerates; red meat isn't bad for you.
s: Cherry picking against the consensus (IARC: processed meat Group 1, red meat Group 2A)
k: Nutrition studies are all observational Saturated fat has been cleared Meat doesn't cause cancer Health and nutrition

t: G14. Ultra-processed vegan foods are worse than meat.
s: False dichotomy: veganism doesn't require ultra-processed foods
k: Vegan meat is full of chemicals I prefer real food Health and nutrition

t: G15. Plants have antinutrients.
s: Doses and preparation make them irrelevant; populations eating plant-based diets live longer
k: Beans have lectins Spinach has oxalates Plants have poisons to defend themselves Health and nutrition

t: G16. Vegans are weak, pale and depressed.
s: A stereotype; the existing correlations have uncertain or reverse causation
k: Every vegan looks sick They're missing meat in their heads Health and nutrition

t: G17. My doctor told me to eat meat.
s: An appeal to individual authority against institutional positions
k: My dietitian said I need it No doctor recommends veganism Health and nutrition

t: H1. Vegans' soy is destroying the Amazon.
s: Most soy becomes animal feed; pasture is the main driver of deforestation
k: Tofu causes deforestation You eat the soy that destroys forests Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H2. Harvests kill animals; vegans kill too.
s: Animal farming uses far more cropland (for feed) and land
k: How many mice died for your salad? Vegans have blood on their hands too Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H3. Regenerative grazing sequesters carbon.
s: Limited, temporary sequestration that cannot scale; it needs more land per calorie
k: Well-managed cattle restore the soil Holistic grazing reverses desertification Carbon-neutral beef Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H4. Cattle graze where crops can't grow.
s: Partly true, but that land could be rewilded and produces few calories
k: Cattle turn grass into food That land is only good for cattle Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H5. Cow methane is biogenic; it doesn't count.
s: Methane has a strong short-term effect; growing herds increase warming
k: Methane disappears in 12 years Cows have always burped Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H6. Avocados and almonds use a lot of water.
s: A selective comparison; per nutrient, animal products lead in water and land use
k: Almond milk dries up rivers Quinoa took food from people in the Andes Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H7. Imported vegan food pollutes in transport.
s: Transport is a small share of emissions; what you eat matters more than how far it traveled
k: Your tofu comes from far away The neighbor's beef pollutes less than imported nuts Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H8. Local, organic meat is sustainable.
s: Grass-fed beef usually needs more land and emits as much or more per kilo
k: I buy organic Grass-fed beef is sustainable Eat local Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H9. Agriculture can't work without manure.
s: Green manures and compost exist; the manure comes from crops grown for feed
k: Without animals there is no fertilizer Organic farming depends on cattle Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H10. Sustainable fishing and aquaculture solve it.
s: Bycatch, overfishing and feed made from wild fish; the suffering continues
k: I buy certified fish Farmed fish don't affect the ocean Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H11. Hunting controls populations.
s: It often causes the imbalance it claims to fix; non-lethal methods exist
k: Wild boars are a pest Without hunting, deer starve Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H12. Livestock pollutes little; the problem is fossil fuels.
s: False dichotomy; food systems account for about a third of emissions
k: The problem is cars Focus on the oil companies Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H13. If meat is sustainable, there's no problem.
s: Reduces a moral question about victims to an environmental one
k: My only issue is deforestation With carbon-neutral meat there is no reason to be vegan Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: H14. Eating insects is the sustainable protein of the future
s: Trades environmental impact for trillions of probable victims; plant proteins are just as efficient, with no one to suffer
k: Cricket flour is eco-friendly Insects don't feel, so farm as many as you like Environment, ecology and agriculture

t: I1. Animal testing has saved millions of lives.
s: A benefit doesn't justify using those who can't consent; translational failure rates are high
k: Would you rather test on children? Without rats there'd be no vaccines Medicine needs it Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I2. If you take medicine, you can't oppose testing.
s: Tu quoque; testing is required by law, not chosen by the patient
k: You take vaccines, so you're not vegan Hypocrite who uses medicine Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I3. Leather is just a byproduct of meat.
s: Profitable byproducts subsidize slaughter
k: The leather would be thrown away Better to use the whole animal Synthetic leather is plastic Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I4. Sheep need to be shorn.
s: Only because they were bred for excessive wool; mulesing, and slaughter when production ends
k: Without shearing, sheep die of heat Wool is natural and sustainable Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I5. Bees make extra honey.
s: Honey is the bees' food reserve; honeybees compete with native pollinators
k: Honey is natural Without beekeepers, bees disappear Bees don't even feel anything Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I6. Zoos conserve species and educate.
s: Few of the species kept are endangered or reintroduced
k: Without zoos, children wouldn't know animals They live longer in zoos Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I7. Aquariums and dolphin parks are harmless.
s: Severe captivity for wide-ranging animals with complex social lives
k: Dolphins enjoy doing shows Aquariums teach about the ocean Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I8. Rodeos, bullfights and circuses are culture.
s: Appeal to tradition (D1) applied to suffering imposed for entertainment
k: Rodeo is cultural heritage They want to end the tradition The bull doesn't even feel it Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I9. Horses like working and being ridden.
s: A convenient projection by those who benefit
k: Horses were born to be ridden The carriage driver depends on it Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I10. In sport fishing the fish is released.
s: Injury, stress and post-release mortality; pain as a pastime
k: I catch and release It's just a little hook Fishing is my therapy Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I11. Having a pet is exploitation too, and your cat eats meat.
s: Adopting and caring differs from breeding to use; cats need nutrients, not meat; and none of this licenses eating animals
k: Then you shouldn't have a dog Neutering is exploitation too Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: I12. Trophy hunting funds conservation.
s: Little money reaches conservation; it uses individuals as tools
k: Hunters are the biggest conservationists The license pays for park rangers Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment

t: J1. Veganism is expensive.
s: Beans, rice, grains and vegetables are among the cheapest foods
k: Vegan food is for the rich Vegan cheese costs a fortune Practicality, economy and society

t: J2. Poor people have no access.
s: A real barrier for some, which doesn't apply to the person objecting; and many cultures have old vegetarian traditions
k: Tell that to people who are going hungry There's no vegan store in poor neighborhoods Veganism is a privilege of white, wealthy people It's a middle-class thing It's for people in city apartments Practicality, economy and society

t: J3. Farmers and slaughterhouse workers would lose their jobs.
s: An argument used against every moral reform; transitions can be planned
k: What about the farmers? You want to put millions out of work Practicality, economy and society

t: J4. Agriculture is the backbone of the economy.
s: Economic importance is not a moral justification; it ignores subsidies and external costs
k: Farming feeds the nation The country lives off agribusiness Veganism would wreck the economy Practicality, economy and society

t: J5. What would we do with the animals if everyone went vegan?
s: A gradual change reduces births; the problem is created by breeding itself
k: Release the cows into the streets? They'd have to kill them all at once Practicality, economy and society

t: J6. There are more important human problems.
s: Priority fallacy: eating plants doesn't take time from any other cause
k: With so many children going hungry... Fight for people first Practicality, economy and society

t: J7. Veganism is a political ideology or a globalist agenda.
s: Guilt by association and conspiracy theory; it doesn't assess the argument
k: It's a leftist thing They want us to eat bugs They want to control what you eat Practicality, economy and society

t: J9. It's hard; I don't have time.
s: Initial difficulty isn't impossibility; inconvenience doesn't justify harm
k: I work all day I can't cook Practicality, economy and society

t: J10. Vegan food is bland.
s: A generalization from unfamiliarity; most spices and many dishes are already plant-based
k: Just salad? Rabbit food Am I supposed to eat grass? Practicality, economy and society

t: J11. Meat tastes good.
s: Taste as a justification for killing: no other context accepts this
k: Bacon is too good I can't live without cheese Steak is sacred Practicality, economy and society

t: J12. I eat little meat; that's enough.
s: Reducing is better than nothing, but it doesn't justify what is left
k: I only eat meat on weekends I do Meatless Monday I'm a flexitarian Practicality, economy and society

t: J13. Eating out, traveling and parties become impossible.
s: Exaggerates the social cost; options keep growing and adapting is quick
k: What about dinner at my in-laws? I'll be left out Practicality, economy and society

t: J14. Fishers and ranchers would lose their identity.
s: Identity doesn't justify harm to others; it calls for a just transition
k: My family has always lived from fishing I'm a rancher's son Practicality, economy and society

t: J15. A vegan world is utopian.
s: Confuses full, immediate feasibility with a present individual duty
k: That will never happen It's a hippie dream Practicality, economy and society

t: K1. One person doesn't make a difference.
s: Expected-value reasoning: the elasticity is below 1 but positive, and buying less leads to producing less
k: It's a drop in the ocean You alone won't change anything Supply and demand don't work like that with meat The slaughterhouse kills the same number anyway The price drops and someone else buys it Effectiveness and individual responsibility

t: K2. The animal is already dead.
s: The purchase pays for restocking, that is, the next death
k: It's already in the store; it'll go to waste I wasn't the one who killed it Effectiveness and individual responsibility

t: K4. There is no ethical consumption under capitalism.
s: A partial truth used to erase huge differences in harm
k: Everything is exploitation Your sneakers were made with slave labor Effectiveness and individual responsibility

t: K5. I'll wait for cultivated meat.
s: Postpones the duty until it costs nothing
k: In ten years technology will fix it When it's cheap, I'll switch Effectiveness and individual responsibility

t: K6. Radical veganism pushes people away.
s: May be a fair point about strategy, but it is neither a moral rebuttal nor a personal excuse
k: You scare people off Why don't you just promote reduction? Toxic veganism Effectiveness and individual responsibility

t: K7. I don't kill; I just eat.
s: Outsourced morality: paying for the act is taking part in it
k: I just buy it The butcher is the one who kills Effectiveness and individual responsibility

t: K9. Vegans should fight for laws, not diets.
s: False dichotomy; personal consistency and political action complement each other
k: Diet is individualism Do politics instead of pestering people Effectiveness and individual responsibility

t: L1. Vegans are annoying and think they are better.
s: Ad hominem: the messenger's behavior doesn't change whether the message is valid
k: How do you know someone's vegan? They'll tell you You think you are better than us Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L2. Veganism is a cult, a religion.
s: A label used to avoid evaluating; veganism rests on public arguments
k: You preach like fanatics That's indoctrination Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L3. Hitler was a vegetarian.
s: Reductio ad Hitlerum and guilt by association; historically doubtful
k: Hitler loved animals The Nazis passed animal protection laws Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L4. You use a phone, so you're a hypocrite.
s: Tu quoque: someone's inconsistency doesn't make what they say false
k: You drive a car What about tires with animal fat? Your phone has minerals mined by children Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L5. Veganism isn't 100% cruelty-free.
s: Nirvana fallacy: reducing harm doesn't require eliminating it entirely
k: No vegan is 100% vegan So veganism doesn't exist Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L6. Vegans care more about animals than people.
s: False dilemma and generalization; empathy is not a zero-sum resource
k: You cry for the cow but not for the homeless Vegans hate people Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L7. Comparing animal farming to slavery or the Holocaust is offensive.
s: Distinguish structural analogy from moral equivalence; handle with care and sources
k: You trivialize the Holocaust That comparison is racist Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L8. If vegans eat fake meat, they want meat.
s: The problem was never the taste; it was the victim
k: Why call it a burger? A vegan sausage is a contradiction Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L9. I'll eat double to make up for you.
s: An emotional reaction (reactance), not an argument
k: I'll eat some bacon in your honor For every vegan, one more steak Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L10. Most vegans give up.
s: Difficulty sticking to it says nothing about whether it is right
k: Almost everyone goes back to eating meat Not even you can stick with it Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L11. Vegan activists are radicals and extremists.
s: Judging a cause by the methods of a minority
k: Eco-terrorists Vegans break into farms Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L12. Meat is for real men.
s: A gender stereotype; masculinity is neither a moral nor a nutritional criterion
k: Real men eat meat Salad is for women Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: L13. Veganism is just a fad diet
s: Confuses an ethical position about not harming animals with a menu chosen for health or looks
k: Veganism is a trend It's just another diet; it'll pass Attacks on veganism and vegans

t: V1. Going vegan will make you healthier.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's imprecise: any badly planned diet carries risks.
k: Borrowed reason

t: V2. Veganism would end world hunger.
s: Weak vegan argument: It ignores that hunger is largely a problem of distribution and political will, not just of farm output.
k: Borrowed reason

t: V3. Go vegan for the planet.
s: Weak vegan argument: The problem isn't that the environmental argument is false. It's that it is fragile exactly where it most needs to be solid: if the reason to reject animal farming is its environmental impact, cleaner animal farming would solve the problem without solving anything for the animals.
k: Borrowed reason

t: V4. Meat eaters are psychopaths.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's inaccurate and counterproductive. Most of these people have genuine emotional bonds.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V5. There's no such thing as an ex-vegan.
s: Weak vegan argument: Being vegan is an ethical position held up by arguments and repeated choices, not a genetic trait. Any such position can be abandoned. There are ex-abolitionists, ex-feminists and ex-pacifists for the same reason.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V6. Using force to protect animals is always wrong.
s: Weak vegan argument: The question is more open than that certainty suggests. Absolute pacifism trips over its own logic: refusing to stop a greater harm, in practice, lets it happen. And we accept forceful intervention for humans who cannot defend themselves, such as a child being attacked.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V7. Being vegan is very expensive.
s: Weak vegan argument: Coming from a vegan, the phrase confirms one of the myths most used against veganism, and pushes away people who might join.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V8. Anemia mostly affects meat eaters.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's a base-rate fallacy: since most people eat meat, most cases of almost anything occur among meat eaters. That doesn't show that meat causes anemia.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V9. Every nutrition body in the world approves vegan diets for everyone.
s: Weak vegan argument: It overstates the consensus. The US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and the British Dietetic Association say well-planned vegan diets can be appropriate at every stage of life. But the German Nutrition Society, in 2024, neither recommended nor advised against vegan diets for pregnant women, children and older adults, for lack of data, and European pediatric bodies are cautious.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V10. Doctors don't know anything about nutrition.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's a generalization. Nutrition training in medical school is often short, but that doesn't mean no doctor understands the subject, and many specialize in it.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V11. In India almost everyone is vegan.
s: Weak vegan argument: It confuses vegetarianism with veganism. About 39% of Indian adults say they are vegetarian, and milk consumption in the country is very high.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V12. Each vegan saves 200 animals a year.
s: Weak vegan argument: The number looks precise, but it's a simple division: total animals killed divided by the number of people. It ignores that production doesn't fall in the same proportion as demand, because prices drop and others buy part of what was not bought.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V13. Hitler wasn't even really a vegetarian.
s: Weak vegan argument: Hitler's diet is debated by historians, and answering on historical grounds unintentionally accepts that it would matter to the discussion.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V14. All animals are slaughtered fully conscious, without stunning.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's a generalization. In the European Union and in Brazil, the law requires stunning cattle, pigs and poultry before bleeding, and in the United States federal law requires it for mammals, though not for poultry. Most slaughter follows these rules, even with failures and exceptions.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V15. Jesus was a vegetarian.
s: Weak vegan argument: The Gospels describe Jesus eating and offering fish, and the theories that he was vegetarian, for example through a link with the Essenes, have no solid historical basis.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V16. Great geniuses like Einstein and Da Vinci were vegan.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's the same appeal to authority as the opposing argument, just from the other side. If the diet of famous thinkers doesn't prove that eating meat is right, it doesn't prove that not eating it is either.
k: Exaggeration or attack

t: V17. God didn't make animals for humans.
s: Weak vegan argument: Religious arguments of this kind depend on belief, not on reasons anyone can share, so they don't persuade people of a different faith.
k: Wrong criterion

t: V18. We should love animals.
s: Weak vegan argument: It confuses affection with respect. No one is obliged to love humans or animals, but no one has the right to harm them for that reason.
k: Wrong criterion

t: V19. Humans come first.
s: Weak vegan argument: As a general principle, it is plain speciesism, whether applied by vegans or non-vegans.
k: Wrong criterion

t: V20. I'm vegan out of compassion for all living beings.
s: Weak vegan argument: Veganism's criterion isn't being alive, it's being sentient. Plants, fungi and single-celled organisms are alive, but there's no evidence they can be harmed in the sense that matters.
k: Wrong criterion

t: V21. Pigs are smarter than a three-year-old child.
s: Weak vegan argument: The comparison is widely shared but rests on weak studies. The experiment in which pigs used a mirror to find food has not been replicated, and comparing the intelligence of species by a single measure has no solid basis.
k: Wrong criterion

t: V22. Comparing it to slavery pushes people away.
s: Weak vegan argument: It can look like a strategic concern. The test is simple: if it were shown that the comparison is more effective at improving the situation of animals, would you start supporting it? If the answer is no, the objection was always moral, just dressed up as tactics.
k: Objection in disguise

t: V23. Don't show the footage; it's too shocking.
s: Weak vegan argument: At some point this caution becomes an inverted priority: it treats the discomfort of the viewer as more important than the suffering of those being filmed.
k: Objection in disguise

t: V24. This partial law is unfair to the other animals.
s: Weak vegan argument: It sounds like an even stronger commitment, but it proves too much: since it's impossible to ban every form of exploitation at once, someone who cares about outcomes would prefer a real reduction in suffering to none.
k: Objection in disguise

t: V25. Not your mom, not your milk.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's an appeal to nature: it suggests milk from another species is wrong because nature didn't reserve it for us. Natural doesn't define right, and vegans point out this same mistake in "it's natural to eat meat".
k: A fact with no moral weight

t: V26. Eggs are chicken periods.
s: Weak vegan argument: Even if the comparison were accurate, it says nothing moral. Being gross doesn't make something wrong, and not being gross wouldn't make it right. The listener can simply say they don't care.
k: A fact with no moral weight

t: V27. No adult animal drinks milk.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's an appeal to nature. We do many things no other animal does, like cooking, and that doesn't make them wrong; other animals not drinking milk doesn't make milk wrong either.
k: A fact with no moral weight

t: V28. Meat eaters eat more soy than vegans.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's true that about three quarters of the world's soy becomes animal feed, and that is a good argument about deforestation.
k: A fact with no moral weight

t: V29. Cats can't be vegan.
s: Weak vegan argument: Many vegans repeat this as if it were established fact, but the available evidence points the other way. In a study of 1,369 cats published in PLOS ONE in 2023, the 127 fed a vegan diet tended to be as healthy or healthier on all seven general indicators, and a 2021 study of more than a thousand cats in Canada and the US also found no harm. A vegan cat food tested at the Federal University of Lavras, in Brazil, met the cats' needs on the measures assessed.
k: Weak or false science

t: V30. Humans are biologically herbivores.
s: Weak vegan argument: It isn't an ethical argument. It suggests we should be vegan because we can't make use of meat, milk and eggs, not because exploiting animals is wrong.
k: Weak or false science

t: V31. Vegans are sexier and better in bed.
s: Weak vegan argument: It takes the focus off the animals and appeals to the listener's self-interest.
k: Weak or false science

t: V32. Broccoli and spinach have more protein than meat.
s: Weak vegan argument: The confusion comes from charts that count protein per calorie, not per weight. About half of spinach's calories come from protein, but it has very few calories: 100 g provides only about 3 g of protein.
k: Weak or false science

t: V33. Vegans don't need to supplement B12.
s: Weak vegan argument: It is irresponsible and can put people's health at risk. Calling supplementation "a pharmaceutical industry scam" is a conspiracy claim with no evidence.
k: Weak or false science

t: V34. Gorillas, bulls and horses get strong eating only plants.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's a false analogy. Cattle digest grass with the help of microbes in the rumen, and horses ferment fiber in the large intestine; the microbes turn fiber and other compounds into nutrients, including protein. Gorillas spend much of the day eating large volumes of leaves and have a gut adapted to ferment them. The human digestive system doesn't work like that.
k: Weak or false science

t: V35. All the B12 in meat comes from supplements.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's an exaggeration. Farmed pigs and chickens get B12 in their feed, but in cattle B12 is produced by bacteria in the rumen from cobalt, which doesn't always need to be added.
k: Weak or false science

t: V36. Livestock pollutes more than all cars, planes and ships combined.
s: Weak vegan argument: The phrase comes from the 2006 FAO report, which compared livestock's 18% of emissions with about 13% for transport. But the accounting differed: for livestock it counted the whole chain, from feed to slaughter; for transport, only fuel combustion. One of the authors acknowledged the problem in 2010.
k: Weak or false science

t: V37. Livestock causes 51% of the world's greenhouse gas emissions.
s: Weak vegan argument: The figure comes from a 2009 piece published by the Worldwatch Institute, which counted, for example, animal respiration, something international methodologies do not count as emissions. It became famous through the documentary *Cowspiracy*.
k: Weak or false science

t: V38. Animal testing is useless: 90% of drugs fail.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's an exaggeration. About 90% of drug candidates fail in human trials, and species differences are one of the causes. But failures have many other causes, and the figure doesn't prove that tests have never helped.
k: Weak or false science

t: V39. Unseasoned meat tastes of nothing; all the flavor comes from seasoning.
s: Weak vegan argument: It's an exaggeration. Meat has its own flavor, which comes from fat, from compounds like heme iron and from the reactions that happen when it browns.
k: Weak or false science

t: V40. It's proven that vegans are more empathetic.
s: Weak vegan argument: The claim usually relies on a 2010 neuroimaging study of 60 people, which measured brain activation in response to images, not behavior. It is modest evidence, not proof.
k: Weak or false science

t: V41. Koko the gorilla held conversations in sign language.
s: Weak vegan argument: Koko learned many signs, but the claim that she used a language, with grammar and new sentences, does not hold up: the interpretation depended heavily on her trainers.
k: Weak or false science

t: V42. It's proven that meat played no role in human evolution.
s: Weak vegan argument: It overstates a real study. Barr and colleagues showed in 2022 that the apparent increase in evidence of meat-eating in the time of *Homo erectus* disappears once research effort is accounted for. That weakens one hypothesis, but it doesn't prove meat played no role.
k: Weak or false science

t: V43. Science proves veganism is right.
s: Weak vegan argument: Science answers questions of fact, such as whether animals feel pain and whether a vegan diet can be healthy. Whether it is right to cause that suffering is a moral question, which no study answers on its own.
k: Weak or false science

t: V44. Oysters and mussels feel pain like any other animal.
s: Weak vegan argument: The evidence of sentience in bivalves is weak: they have very simple nervous systems with no centralized brain, and even animal advocates admit they may not feel.
k: Weak or false science

t: V45. Cultivated meat isn't vegan, because it comes from animals.
s: Weak vegan argument: The definitional objection confuses the letter of the commitment with its spirit: veganism is not a closed list of forbidden ingredients, it is a commitment to ending unnecessary harm to sentient beings.
k: Purity and invented rules

t: V46. Food that may contain traces of milk isn't vegan.
s: Weak vegan argument: "May contain traces" is a warning for people with allergies: the product went through machines that also process that ingredient. The ingredient isn't in the recipe.
k: Purity and invented rules

t: V47. A good vegan only eats natural, organic, healthy food.
s: Weak vegan argument: Nothing in vegan ethics requires that. The concern is not exploiting animals, whether dinner is an organic salad or French fries.
k: Purity and invented rules

t: V48. On a desert island, I'd starve before eating an animal.
s: Weak vegan argument: The very definition of veganism speaks of avoiding exploitation "as far as is possible and practicable". In a real survival situation, not eating an animal may be beyond what is possible, and saying otherwise creates a demand veganism does not make.
k: Purity and invented rules

t: V49. I'm vegan, but I taste the food when I visit my family.
s: Weak vegan argument: If the reason not to eat animals is the animal, it doesn't change because the table belongs to your family. For whoever died, the occasion makes no difference.
k: A concession that empties the point

t: V50. I'm vegan, but I don't think everyone should be.
s: Weak vegan argument: It treats as personal taste something that has a victim. No one says "I'm against assaulting people, but I don't think everyone should be." If the harm is unjust when you cause it, it is also unjust when someone else does.
k: A concession that empties the point

t: V51. Being vegan requires being anti-capitalist.
s: Weak vegan argument: When someone says this without saying, just as firmly, that anti-capitalists should be vegan, the real goal isn't animal welfare. It's recruiting supporters for another cause from inside the vegan movement.
k: The cause as a tool

t: V52. More expensive meat is bad for ordinary people.
s: Weak vegan argument: When the price of animal products rises, the drop in consumption is usually treated only as sad news, and not also as what it is: fewer animals killed.
k: The cause as a tool

t: V53. Veganism is only about animals; nothing else matters.
s: Weak vegan argument: Veganism does focus on animal exploitation, but that's no license to treat other humans unfairly or with prejudice. Humans are sentient too, and the criterion applies to them.
k: The cause as a tool

t: Antispeciesism and sentientism
s: Beyond veganism: Veganism is one consequence of a broader criterion: what matters morally is the capacity to be harmed or benefited.

t: The state of the art in animal ethics
s: Beyond veganism: Since 1975, animal ethics has been tested on ever harder cases, by authors from schools that disagree with each other, and has reached the same rejection of speciesism.

t: Wild animal suffering
s: Beyond veganism: Hunger, disease and predation were not caused by us. But if sentience is what matters, this suffering cannot be dismissed just because it is natural.

t: Sentience in AI and robots
s: Beyond veganism: No current system is recognized as sentient. But the possibility is not absurd, and the criterion does not depend on what a being is made of.

t: The definition of veganism, debated
s: Beyond veganism: What defines veganism: refusing the exploitation of animals, or refusing everything of animal origin? The question has come back strongly with cultivated meat and precision fermentation.

t: Sentience in extraterrestrial beings
s: Beyond veganism: There is no evidence of life beyond Earth, let alone sentient life. The question tests whether our criterion is really a criterion, or just a preference for our own species.

t: Liberalism: Freedom is a right of rational individuals; animals aren't subjects of liberal rights.
s: Political objection: Protect individuals against harm caused by others and ensure each can live their own life. For Mill, the only legitimate reason to limit someone's freedom is to prevent harm to others.
k: politics theory

t: Libertarianism and anarcho-capitalism: What's mine is mine: animals are property, and the freedom to use property is sacred.
s: Political objection: Self-ownership and the non-aggression principle: no one may initiate violence against another individual.
k: politics theory

t: Marxism, socialism and communism: Exploitation is a relation between human classes. Animals aren't workers, and the struggle is a different one.
s: Political objection: End exploitation and the turning of beings and lives into commodities.
k: politics theory

t: Anarchism: Anarchism fights domination between people; animals are not part of that.
s: Political objection: Reject hierarchies and forms of domination that cannot be justified.
k: politics theory

t: Utilitarianism: Human pleasures are worth more: better to be a human dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.
s: Political objection: Maximize well-being and minimize suffering for everyone affected, counting each one's interest equally.
k: politics theory

t: Contractualism and Rawlsian justice: Justice holds among those who have a sense of justice and can make agreements.
s: Political objection: Choose the rules of a society impartially, as if we did not know what position we would occupy in it.
k: politics theory

t: Deontology and Kantianism: Only rational beings are ends in themselves; toward animals we have, at most, indirect duties.
s: Political objection: Treat beings who have value of their own as ends, and never merely as means.
k: politics theory

t: Communitarianism: Duties arise from the community and its traditions, and animals are not members of it.
s: Political objection: Morality is built in the bonds and practices of a community.
k: politics theory

t: Egalitarianism and prioritarianism: Equality is among human citizens; animals belong to another category.
s: Political objection: Reduce unjust inequalities and give priority to those who are worst off.
k: politics theory

t: Ethics of care: Care applies to close relationships, not to unknown animals.
s: Political objection: Respond to the needs of the vulnerable and the dependent with attention and responsibility.
k: politics theory

t: Virtue ethics: Virtue is about human character; treating animals well matters only because it makes us better.
s: Political objection: Cultivate virtues like compassion, justice and temperance, and avoid vices like cruelty.
k: politics theory

t: Feminism: Feminism is about women; talking about cows and hens is changing the subject, or even offensive.
s: Political objection: End oppression linked to sex and control over the body and reproduction.
k: politics theory

t: Anti-racism, anti-ableism and the fight against other discrimination: Comparing speciesism to racism or ableism is offensive; they are different things.
s: Political objection: Do not give less weight to someone's interests because of a trait that does not change how much they can be harmed, such as race, disability, origin or appearance.
k: politics theory

t: The progressive left and multiculturalism: The animal cause is a white middle-class concern that ends up attacking the cultural practices of minorities.
s: Political objection: Defend vulnerable groups, fight domination and respect cultural diversity.
k: politics theory

t: Pacifism and nonviolence: Nonviolence is a commitment between people, not to animals.
s: Political objection: Refuse violence as a means of resolving conflicts and reaching goals.
k: politics theory

t: Effective altruism: Resources for doing good are limited, and should go to humans first.
s: Political objection: Use evidence and reason to do the most good possible with the resources available.
k: politics theory

t: Family A: Sentience and moral status
s: Do animals count morally?

t: Family B: Harm, death and welfare
s: Does killing without suffering harm the individual?

t: Family C: Nature, biology and evolution
s: Is what is natural justified?

t: Family D: Tradition, culture and religion
s: Does custom justify it?

t: Family E: Relativism, freedom and evasions
s: Is it just a matter of choice?

t: Family F: Edge cases and hypotheticals
s: What about the desert island?

t: Family G: Health and nutrition
s: Do we need animal products?

t: Family H: Environment, ecology and agriculture
s: Is veganism worse for the planet?

t: Family I: Other uses: testing, clothing, entertainment
s: And beyond the plate?

t: Family J: Practicality, economy and society
s: Is it feasible and fair to ask this?

t: Family K: Effectiveness and individual responsibility
s: Does my choice change anything?

t: Family L: Attacks on veganism and vegans
s: Can the people saying this be trusted?

t: Appeal to nature
s: Fallacy: "It's natural, so it's good"

t: Hume's law (from is to ought)
s: Fallacy: Deriving a norm from a fact

t: Appeal to tradition
s: Fallacy: "It's always been this way"

t: Appeal to popularity and normality
s: Fallacy: "Everybody does it"

t: Appeal to authority
s: Fallacy: "So-and-so said it or did it"

t: Arbitrary criterion (speciesism)
s: Fallacy: An irrelevant trait chosen as the moral boundary

t: Persuasive definition
s: Fallacy: Defining the term to win the argument

t: Begging the question
s: Fallacy: The conclusion is hidden in the premise

t: Continuum fallacy
s: Fallacy: No exact line means no difference

t: Hasty generalization from an exception
s: Fallacy: An exception used as the rule

t: False dichotomy
s: Fallacy: Either this or that, with no third way

t: Nirvana fallacy
s: Fallacy: If it isn't perfect, it doesn't count

t: Tu quoque
s: Fallacy: "You do it too"

t: Ad hominem and poisoning the well
s: Fallacy: Attacking the person

t: Guilt by association
s: Fallacy: Linking the idea to something hated

t: Priority fallacy
s: Fallacy: "There are more important things"

t: Anecdotal evidence
s: Fallacy: One case against the data

t: Cherry picking
s: Fallacy: Selecting only the favorable data

t: False middle ground
s: Fallacy: The truth is always in the middle

t: Changing the question (red herring)
s: Fallacy: Swapping "is it wrong?" for another question

t: Cognitive dissonance (the meat paradox)
s: Bias: Loving animals and eating them creates tension, resolved by denying minds to the animals eaten (Bastian et al., 2012)

t: Motivated reasoning
s: Bias: Looking for reasons for the conclusion you already want

t: Confirmation bias
s: Bias: Accepting only what confirms a prior belief

t: Status quo bias
s: Bias: Preferring the current state because it is current

t: System justification
s: Bias: Legitimizing the existing order to reduce discomfort

t: Willful ignorance
s: Bias: Avoiding information that would create an obligation

t: Functional categorization
s: Bias: "Food" animals are granted less mind than "pet" animals

t: Ingroup bias
s: Bias: Valuing "our own" and devaluing outsiders

t: Scope insensitivity
s: Bias: Billions of victims don't weigh more than one

t: Diffusion of responsibility
s: Bias: Shared blame feels like no blame

t: Psychological reactance
s: Bias: Pushing back when freedom feels threatened

t: Identity-protective cognition
s: Bias: Rejecting ideas that threaten the group or one's identity

t: Affect heuristic
s: Bias: "I like it, so it's good"

t: Moral licensing
s: Bias: One good act licenses a bad one

t: Optimism bias and exceptionalism
s: Bias: "My meat is different"

t: Survivorship bias
s: Bias: We only see those who made it

t: The 4Ns rationalization
s: Bias: Justifying eating animals by saying it is natural, normal, necessary and nice (Piazza and colleagues, 2015).

t: Hypocrisy hunting
s: Bias: Looking for an inconsistency in whoever defends an idea so as not to examine the idea.

t: Mind denial
s: Bias: Attributing less mind and less capacity to suffer to the animals we eat.

t: Do-gooder derogation
s: Bias: Belittling people who act for moral reasons, because their conduct feels like an accusation.

t: Reactive devaluation
s: Bias: Rejecting a proposal because it came from the other side.

t: Messenger effect
s: Bias: Judging the message by who says it rather than by what it says.

t: Bandwagon effect and social conformity
s: Bias: Adopting a habit or an idea because many people around you do.

t: Pluralistic ignorance
s: Bias: Many disagree in private but think everyone else agrees.

t: Default effect
s: Bias: Sticking with the option that comes ready-made, like the plate with meat.

t: Illusory truth and mere exposure effects
s: Bias: What you hear often seems true, and what is familiar seems better.

t: Omission bias and perpetrator bias
s: Bias: Judging as less serious the harm we don't cause with our own hands, or that results from not acting.

t: Teleological bias and agency detection
s: Bias: Seeing purpose and intention in nature: animals would "exist for" something.

t: Collapse of compassion
s: Bias: The more victims, the less we feel for each; one identifiable victim moves us more than millions.

t: Loss aversion and the endowment effect
s: Bias: Losing what you have weighs more than gaining something equivalent.

t: Sunk cost and effort justification
s: Bias: Carrying on because you've invested a lot, not because it's worth it.

t: Rosy retrospection
s: Bias: Remembering the past as better than it was.

t: Overconfidence (Dunning-Kruger)
s: Bias: People who know little about a topic tend to overestimate what they know.

t: Naive realism and the bias blind spot
s: Bias: Thinking we see the world as it is and only others are biased.

t: Anthropocentric thinking
s: Bias: Using humans as the measure of everything, including of what counts as feeling.

t: Naturalness bias
s: Bias: What seems natural is judged better and safer.

t: Availability bias
s: Bias: Judging by the easiest memory, like an acquaintance's case, rather than by the data.

t: Authority bias
s: Bias: Accepting a claim because of the prestige of whoever makes it.

t: Present bias
s: Bias: Giving too much weight to now and too little to future consequences.

t: Halo effect
s: Bias: One good quality, like "local" or "organic", colors the judgment of everything else.

t: Social dominance orientation
s: Bias: Preferring hierarchies between groups, including between species.

t: Psychological essentialism
s: Bias: Believing each kind of being has a fixed essence that defines its place.

t: Masculinity and meat
s: Bias: Associating eating meat with manliness, which makes change feel like a threat to identity.

t: Stereotyping
s: Bias: Judging someone by a simplified image of the group they belong to.

t: Dissociation and euphemism
s: Bias: Separating the animal from the food, including through the words we use.

t: False consensus
s: Bias: Overestimating how many people think like us.

t: Food neophobia
s: Bias: Distrusting unfamiliar foods.

t: Nocebo effect
s: Bias: Expecting something to do harm produces real symptoms.

t: Salience bias
s: Bias: Giving weight to what grabs attention, like the distance traveled, rather than to what matters most.

t: Middle-ground bias
s: Bias: Thinking the middle position is always the most sensible.
